headline: RBA hike of 25bp justified by materialisation of upside inflation risks: oil prices near $100/barrel, productivity weakness, AI-driven capacity pressures and CPI still well above 3%
reasoning: Lomas was not fully convinced a hike was coming but the RBA delivered 25bp, citing materialisation of upside inflation risks. Key drivers include the US-Iran conflict keeping oil prices around or above $100/barrel, persistent productivity and capacity constraints, the AI and data centre boom adding demand pressure to an already capacity-constrained economy, and headline inflation still sitting well above 3%. These factors combined to justify the move in the RBA's view.
quote: I wasn't convinced they were going to raise the rates today, but they have, as, as you would know already, 0.25 percentage points. And the justification is really around the materialisation of upside risks, as in upside to pushing inflation higher. We've been watching for the last couple of weeks the US conflict with Iran continuing to escalate. And along with that, the oil price has been well and truly kind of hovering around the $100 remark or slightly above $100 a barrel. And then that's that's flowing through not just to Australia, but all, all across the world. There's the ongoing issue with productivity, which the other way to describe it is really around capacity. And so the Reserve Bank has highlighted that those capacity pressures are still very much at the forefront of their mind, highlights the importance of continuing to lift productivity. And then you've got AI and data centres. So all of those those things coming together as well as inflation still sitting well and truly above 3% is the justification for the rate rise.

headline: Was not convinced a rate hike was warranted, citing declining housing market, flat household spending, rising unemployment to 4.6%, and incomplete pass-through of prior rate rises
reasoning: Amy Lomas argued against the RBA's hike decision, pointing to a sharper-than-expected decline in the housing market, flat (or slightly falling) household spending when abstracting for fuel prices, and August unemployment rising to 4.6% — within the RBA/Treasury's non-inflationary range of 4.25–5%. She noted consumer sentiment was weak and that previous rate rises had not yet fully washed through the economy, suggesting a hefty list of factors already working against inflation. She acknowledged the RBA was trying to get ahead of inflation expectations, particularly around Middle East oil price risks.
quote: The reason I wasn't convinced is that there's a lot that's happening in the economy which takes pressure off inflation. So the sharper than expected decline in the housing market, retail spending, I mean, retail spending is a good indicator of consumer spending. The consumer spending, the household data that came out today, which shows that if you abstract for fuel prices, household spending was flat. In fact it fell slightly and then the unemployment lifted, unemployment rate, sorry, for August lifted to 4.6%. And when you look at the sort of range where Treasury and the Commonwealth Government, sorry, Treasury and the Reserve Bank believe that unemployment needs to be at in order to not be driving inflation, it's somewhere between 4.25% and 5%. So an August reading of 4.6 would suggest you sort of in there somewhere as well.

headline: AI productivity gains for Australia are real but delayed — analogous to the mining boom, where productivity only materialised once exports began, not during construction
reasoning: Lomas argued that the AI productivity dividend will eventually come to Australia but will take time, drawing a parallel to the mining boom where productivity gains only materialised at the export phase, not during the construction build-out. She cautioned against expecting the US to capture all AI productivity gains while Australia sees none — it will arrive, just later. In the meantime, government and business both need to invest more in productivity broadly, including reducing red tape and improving approvals processes.
quote: I think the first thing is not here yet because we can't have this big build out in data centres and adoption of AI and expect that the US is going to be able to get the productivity gains. And we're not going to see any of it. I mean, we will see it. It's just going to take time. And it's like the mining boom. And I mean the mining boom when it was all the construction, you didn't see productivity. It was once you started exporting that you saw. And it's going to be the same here that we probably won't, we won't be seeing the productivity gains until later on.

headline: EV purchases flattered discretionary consumption; stripping them out would leave household spending closer to 0.1% — signalling underlying consumer weakness rather than buoyancy
reasoning: Lomas explains that EV purchases sit in the discretionary consumption bucket but should not be read as a sign of consumer confidence because households are buying them to manage volatile fuel costs rather than out of genuine optimism. The rest of household consumption data was muted, with EVs as the clear standout. Stripping out EVs would have left the quarterly consumption figure near 0.1%, suggesting household spending is not particularly buoyant, which is important context for the RBA.
quote: when you looked at the rest of the household consumption data, it was pretty muted. Actually. The EVs were the stand out. So I think if you'd taken the EVs out to your point, it would have been closer to 0.1%. And on balance, that would suggest that household spending, it's not particularly buoyant, which is obviously pretty important going forward in terms of the RBA thinking about how much strength is there in household consumption when it's thinking about the cash rate and inflation.

headline: November rate rise likely as the peak, not this month; key catalysts are September quarter CPI in late October, dwelling commencements data, and sustained oil prices around $97
reasoning: Lomas does not expect a rate rise in the current month, picking November as the likely timing for a further hike, a view she has held for some time against consensus expectations of cuts. She cites three catalysts: first, the September quarter CPI data due in late October will give the RBA firmer inflation guidance beyond the still-bedding-in monthly series. Second, housing prices have fallen faster and deeper than expected and the flow-through to dwelling commencements needs to be assessed. Third, oil prices near $97 add an inflationary risk that the RBA will want to monitor for persistence before acting.
quote: I don't think we're likely to see a rate rise this month and my pick I think along with a number of economists is likely to be November... The second thing goes to housing. So housing prices have fallen faster and deeper than anybody expected... And then the big kicker is oil prices which are up at around $97.00. Will, I guess the longer we can see whether those gradual or the gradual uptick in oil prices is sustained, then when you bring all of those things together, I think the Reserve Bank would have a much better feel for whether there's another rate rise in the mix or not.

headline: June quarter GDP of 0.4% (2.1% annual) beat expectations but for the wrong reasons: EV-driven household consumption, energy stockpile drawdowns, and stalled productivity (output +2.1% vs hours worked +2.7%)
reasoning: Amy Lomas notes that while the June quarter GDP print of 0.4% (2.1% annual) surprised to the upside versus market expectations of around 0.1–0.2%, the composition is concerning. Household consumption was boosted by EV purchases as a hedge against rising petrol costs, not genuine consumer buoyancy. Export volumes of energy products like coal and LNG rose but required drawing down stockpiles rather than increased production. Productivity stalled, with output growth entirely explained by additional hours worked, implying no efficiency gains.
quote: just because we've had a stronger than expected quarterly out turn for GDP, so that was GDP to the end of the June quarter doesn't mean that we have a strong economy. So when you unpack what contributed to the GDP result, which came in at 0.4% for the quarter and 2.1% for the year and markets were thinking it would be something closer to maybe 0.1% for the quarter or 0.2... When you look at what contributed to that, it was a combination of things that don't really point to a strong economy

headline: Amy Lomas warns further RBA rate rise cannot be ruled out, with oil supply risks and housing construction bottlenecks adding to upside inflation pressure
reasoning: Lomas agrees with the hawkish characterisation, arguing the market is not out of the woods on further rate increases. She highlights geopolitical risk in the Middle East and the potential for oil to spike well above $90/barrel given drawn-down US and Chinese strategic reserves. In addition, she identifies the Australian housing construction pipeline as a persistent inflation driver: rents, utilities and new-build costs have been the biggest contributors over the last 18 months, and the AI construction boom is competing with housing for workers. Her base case for rate cuts is around May next year, but she allows for an earlier start if no further hikes materialise.
quote: I agree, I think that if you look at the statement and you consider what's going on in the world at the moment, I don't think we're out of the woods in terms of there being no further rate increases. I think that there is still the risk of another rate increase. Ah, it's the same reason. It's because we just don't know what's going to happen in the Middle East. And as I mentioned before, reserves have been drawn down. And there is there's a there's a conflict at the moment are in terms of the the outlook for fuel and oil. On one level, the traders are telling us that the prices are unlikely to exceed, you know, $90 a barrel. But when you look at the fundamental supply and demand dynamics, and we think about the level of support that China has provided and the US by drawing down their strategic reserves, and we don't know exactly how much is in reserve, there is a real risk that the prices could really drive back up if the war continues and the disruption to to fuel continues. Um, there's a couple of other things that I've been watching on this front, which I think presents some upside risk. So aside from the Middle East war, while the housing market is a factor in this statement of monetary policy, we're talking about the existing housing market. And when you look at what's been the biggest driver of inflation over the last 18 months or so, it's been housing costs, specifically rents, utilities bills and the cost of building new houses.
